#4580. LiveWire just showed off its biggest electric motorcycle lineup yet

LiveWire has spent the last few years expanding beyond the premium electric motorcycles that originally defined the Harley-Davidson spin-off. But seeing the company’s latest machines all together at EICMA in Milan really drives home just how much broader LiveWire’s ambitions have become.

I stopped by the LiveWire booth at EICMA 2026, where the company had everything from its new lightweight S4 Honcho models to the freshly acquired DUST electric dirt bikes – plus STACYC’s electric balance bikes for the youngest riders.

It’s quite a spread, and perhaps more importantly, it paints a picture of a company that increasingly wants to have an electric two-wheeler for just about every stage of a rider’s life.

I also had a chance to spend several hours test-riding the S4 Honcho Street in Milan, so be on the lookout for that article and video to experience it with me.

But for now, let’s see what was at the LiveWire booth.

Perhaps the most important bikes at the booth were the S4 Honcho models, LiveWire’s new lightweight and lower-cost electric motorcycles.

The production S4 Honcho Street made its European debut at EICMA alongside the dirt-oriented S4 Honcho Trail. The Trail version recently began reaching customers in the US, with the Street now en route to dealerships, and European sales are beginning around the EICMA launch.

These bikes represent a significant departure from LiveWire’s earlier strategy. Instead of trying to compete directly with full-size gasoline motorcycles on outright performance, the Honcho platform is aimed at riders looking for something smaller, simpler, and more approachable.

And now the family is getting even bigger.

Also on display was the new S4 Honcho Skate, making its first public appearance.

The Skate is planned for 2027 and further expands the modular Honcho platform with a stripped-down, playful design.

For those who have followed H-D’s electric ambitions for as long as I have, you might even remember the original Harley-Davidson electric moped prototype that seems to have served as inspiration for the Honcho Skate’s design.

Seeing the various Honcho versions together also makes LiveWire’s strategy with the platform much clearer. Rather than creating one small electric motorcycle, the company is building an entire family around the concept.

The other major attraction at LiveWire’s booth was the DUST lineup.

LiveWire acquired the assets of DUST Moto earlier this year, bringing the lightweight electric dirt bike company under its umbrella. EICMA marked the first public showing of the production-intent DUST Hightail under LiveWire ownership.

The Hightail had already generated plenty of interest before the acquisition as a lightweight, high-performance electric dirt bike. Now we’re getting our first look at how that machine fits into LiveWire’s broader plans.

The company is targeting a 2027 introduction for the production Hightail.

LiveWire also showed the new DUST Spur, another model planned for 2027 and intended to expand the newly formed DUST family.

The DUST acquisition is particularly interesting because it gives LiveWire an immediate foothold in the rapidly growing lightweight electric off-road motorcycle space without having to develop an entirely new platform from scratch.

In what could be a hint at faster charging to come, there was an interesting S2 Alpanista Corsa motorcycle that had been outfitted with a NACS plug and DC fast-charging capabilities.

LiveWire claimed a 20-80% charge in under 10 minutes, which would revolutionize the ability to do long-distance motorcycle touring, or just make it more convenient to get a quick charge and head back to your apartment.

There’s on word on whether the concept will make it to production, but the specs are enticing!

The most interesting part of LiveWire’s EICMA display may not have been any individual motorcycle, but rather what happens when you stand back and look at the entire booth.

On one end you’ve got STACYC electric balance bikes. LiveWire says the brand has already introduced more than 250,000 riders to two wheels.

Then you’ve got the lightweight S4 Honcho family. Above that sit the DUST machines for more serious off-road riding, while LiveWire’s existing S2 motorcycles continue to cover the higher-performance street end of the spectrum.

That’s becoming something of an electric two-wheeler ladder.

A kid can theoretically start on a STACYC, graduate into increasingly capable electric two-wheelers, and eventually wind up on a proper electric motorcycle – all within the same corporate family.

And that feels particularly relevant at a show like EICMA, where much of the motorcycle industry is still trying to figure out exactly where electric motorcycles fit.

LiveWire seems increasingly convinced that the answer isn’t simply to build electric replacements for existing gasoline motorcycles.

Instead, the company is spreading out into categories where electric drivetrains can create different kinds of motorcycles altogether.

I’ve been following LiveWire’s evolution for years, and the company standing in front of me at EICMA looks considerably different from the one that started out selling a single expensive flagship electric motorcycle.

The big, high-performance bikes are still important, but machines like the S4 Honcho and DUST Hightail are arguably more interesting to me because they can bring entirely different riders into electric motorcycling.

They’re smaller. They’re simpler. And perhaps most importantly, they’re targeting the kind of fun, accessible riding that doesn’t require superbike levels of performance.

There’s still plenty we need to learn about several of these new models, particularly final specifications and pricing for the 2027 machines.

But seeing the Honcho, Honcho Skate, Hightail, Spur, and STACYC machines together at EICMA makes one thing pretty clear: LiveWire isn’t just trying to sell a few electric motorcycles anymore.

It’s trying to build an entire electric two-wheeler ecosystem.

#4579. Mayan chieftain named ‘Bat’ ruled over an isolated jungle city

Published Nov 10, 2026 2:33 PM EST

Violent disputes between neighbors and a king named “Bat.” These and other new details about a recently rediscovered, ancient Maya city located in the remote tropical forests of southeast Mexico are beginning to come to light. The approximately 37-acre settlement is so inaccessible that archaeologists initially nicknamed the site Minanbé, or “there is no road” in Yucatec Maya. Despite a challenging journey to the site, researchers have identified multiple building remnants dating back at least 1,100 years. Historical records also indicate heated regional conflicts, and even a local chieftain’s animal-inspired name.

The Mayan Late Classic community was only discovered in May 2026 in the Mexican state Campeche, which shares its southern border with Guatemala. Subsequent hieroglyphic translations from National Autonomous University of Mexico archaeologist Octavio Esparza Olguín, suggest the city’s residents called their settlement Sakil, a Maya term relating to “whiteness.”

Located north of the Calakmul Biosphere Reserve, Minanbé’s surviving structures include religious facilities, palace structures, plazas, water-management systems, and even a nearly 43-foot-tall pyramid. However, archaeologists identified more than architectural features here. After examining 14 pillars and altars, researchers uncovered hieroglyphic records of a violent conflict between Sakil and a rival Mayan hub, Ocomtún. One particular monument’s carved relief depicts a captive lying on his stomach with his wrists tied and head turned sideways. Nearby inscriptions explain the individual was once a resident of Minanbé.

Hieroglyphics on other pillars memorialize a specific regional ruler (kalo’mte’) named Suutz’, which means “bat” in Yucatec Maya. Associated imagery depicts a ruler wearing decorative clothing, sandals, and a detailed headdress. Combined with additional signage, Esparza Olguín and his colleagues believe Suutz’ was a powerful chief who wielded a large amount of authority over Sakil’s residents.

Although the latest archaeological discoveries imply some type of military conflict between Sakil and Ocomtún, it’s still unclear if the problems occurred during the Suutz’ reign. Still, the recent excavations have revealed a great deal in a short amount of time. With more work, the team hopes to learn more about the recently rediscovered settlement, and its residents’ relationship to the world around them.

#4572. This bear’s big butt is so beautiful, it just won an award

Published Nov 10, 2026 3:13 PM EST

Yes, bears are big. Depending on the time of year and sex, the average black bear (Ursus americanus) weighs between 90 to 500 pounds. On average brown bears (Ursus arctos) can weigh between 600 to 900 pounds. However, one female black bear named Volverine is a true fat bear queen this year. The U.S. Forest Service team at Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska have awarded her with the 2026 Big & Beautiful Award for her heft.

The rangers say that this mother bear is a “true icon,” who will often pose on a rock for a long time, seemingly allowing the visitors to Anan Wildlife Observatory to take photos. She is regarded as one of the most beautiful bears at Anan, with a chest patch shaped like the letter V. Volverine is also on the bigger end of the black bear spectrum, with a potato-shaped body, and an especially round butt. Her fishing skills made her one of the largest bears of the 2026 season—and a dominant matriarch.

“Our rangers love to see a fat female bear because that could mean cubs next year!” the rangers write. “Bears have what’s called delayed implantation, meaning they mate in the spring, and IF they get fat enough, the embryos implant in the fall.”

Wishing Volverine and all of the bears the best this winter season.

The rangers at Tongass National Forest are currently awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States, and covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendanhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. The run is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears. Like their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks. Volverine would fit right in with Katmai’s chunky brown bears, despite the fact that black bears tend to be a bit smaller.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of what they are up to 24/7.

#4571. BYD Offices Raided in Legal Probe Over Land Rover Defender Similarities

The BYD Ti7 bears more than a passing resemblance to Land Rover’s current off-road champ, but is that enough to make a case in court?

American buyers may not be familiar with the BYD Ti 7, a Chinese-made three-row hybrid SUV with a boxy shape and an unusual square of painted surface floating above the beltline. They will, however, be familiar with the Land Rover Defender sold in the U.S., a three-row SUV with a boxy shape and an unusual square of painted surface floating above the beltline. And according to a report from British newspaper The Times, Land Rover may have noticed some similarities between the two SUVs.

Last August, according to The Times, a court-ordered raid of BYD’s Dutch offices occurred on behalf of Land Rover company JLR. This was, reportedly, to find documents surrounding how a Land Rover Defender was used in the Ti 7’s development—evidence that could be key in a potential legal case over similarities between the models.

The BYD Ti 7 starts at the equivalent of $27,000 below the MSRP of the most affordable three-row Defenders on the U.K market. It also gets a plug-in hybrid powertrain alongside its seven-seat layout, while Land Rover’s plug-in Defender is only available in England with six seats.

Notably, Land Rover has already been involved in one lawsuit over another automaker attempting to build a product that looks astonishingly similar to a Defender. That model, the Ineos Grenadier, was cleared for sale in 2020 despite looking, well, much like an original Defender.

In the case of the BYD Ti 7, the visual similarities with Land Rover’s larger Defenders are obvious. The question is how much the two SUVs actually have in common, and whether or not it is enough to build a winning legal argument. Top Gear reports that a Dutch court will decide whether a case will proceed later this week.

#4570. Toyota Revives the Scion Name on a Kei Truck for the U.S.

The defunct Scion brand is returning to experiment with new vehicle types, starting with a low-speed kei truck that you probably won't be able to buy.

Apparently, Toyota has been up at night watching Instagram reels. Reading the comments. Scratching its chin. Asking itself an important question: If people are already paying tariffs and other import fees to get old kei trucks into America from Japan, why don’t we just build new ones here?

That brings us to the Scion KEI-01. A small truck. With a tiny engine. And big dreams. What’s essentially a rebadged Daihatsu Hijet Jumbo, the Scion will instead be assembled at the same Toyota plant where the Grand Highlander and Sienna are built, in Princeton, Indiana. The word “kei” comes from the Japanese vehicle classification “keijidōsha,” which translates to light automobile.

See all results for used Toyota for sale near 02895

For now, you won’t find any hiding in the shadow of a lifted Toyota Tundra TRD Pro on dealer lots. Instead, these trucks—shorter than a Mazda MX-5 Miata—will be sold next year through a fleet-focused trial program to test the waters. If demand is strong, Toyota says limited retail sales could follow.

The Scion KEI-01 is as adorable as it looks and is said to weigh less than 2000 pounds, despite having all-wheel drive. Power comes from a tiny 660-cc three-cylinder engine paired with a continuously variable automatic transmission. It uses an independent front suspension, a solid rear axle, and a hydromechanical clutch to automatically shift power between the front and rear wheels based on traction needs. There’s also a “Lock” button to keep power evenly distributed between both axles.

The example Toyota showcased at a media event was equipped with tiny 145/80-12 Yokohama Super Van 355 tires. Its four-lug steel wheels, which almost hide the rear drum brakes, are roughly two inches smaller in diameter than the front brake rotors on the GR Corolla.

Here’s the catch. Just like another mini car—the Fiat Topolino—the Scion is restricted to low-speed duty, effectively making it a mullet-shaped golf cart. Top speed is limited to just 25 mph. Engineers tell us they baked this into the engine’s computer, and a simple “cut the wire” trick won’t unlock highway speeds. Its lack of speed is exactly how Toyota managed to get the KEI-01 into the U.S. so quickly. By meeting federal low-speed vehicle safety requirements, it can avoid the crash-test standards required of conventional passenger vehicles and pickups, retain its right-hand-drive layout, and stay as cute as a button.

See all results for used Toyota for sale near 02895

Measuring just over 11 feet long and less than five feet wide, the KEI-01 features a three-way folding cargo bed that can haul up to 600 pounds. That bed measures six feet six inches if you include the area under the cab, or five feet five inches without.

It comes with air conditioning, reclining seats, and push-button ignition. It will be sold with a cab-mounted reverse camera and may offer a towing package as optional equipment. Yes, it’s got airbags, though not many. Full pricing and options are still very TBD, as production is slated to begin in mid 2027.

The future of the Scion brand has also begun to take shape as a “freedom lab.” Toyota is using the name not as a conventional reboot, but as an outlet for experimental mobility ideas, such as a truck that measures just 11 feet in length.

Alongside the KEI-01, Toyota showed off its SxS Concept (previously revealed at SEMA last year), a side-by-side off-roader packing a turbocharged hybrid inline-four engine with more than 300 horsepower, and the BKE Concept scooter that already looks leagues more comfortable to ride than Honda’s Motocompacto.

It might not initially look like it, but the KEI-01 fits rather comfortably as a Scion. The original Scion brand spent its first life trying to convince young people to buy Toyotas. They wanted people to swap wheels, add racing stripes, and personalize an affordable car. That’s exactly what many people already do with their kei trucks. Just ask the guy baking wood-fired pizzas from the back of his Subaru Sambar if tiny trucks are any fun.

#4569. Musk admits Tesla doesn’t have enough talent to build more than one car at a time after exodus

Elon Musk now says Tesla can’t build the Cybertruck and the Cybercab at the same time because there are only so many “smart, dedicated people” to go around. Half the executives he showed off in 2023 as proof of Tesla’s “bench strength” have since left the company.

It’s the most honest explanation yet for how Tesla went from five consumer vehicle programs at the start of 2026 to a single platform, Model 3 and Model Y, by the middle of 2027.

On Friday, Musk said Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas around the middle of next year “to make room for increased Cybercab production.” As we pointed out at the time, Giga Texas isn’t short on space. The Cybertruck line runs at a fraction of its installed capacity because the truck sells a fraction of what Tesla planned.

A day later, replying to a user on X, Musk gave a different reason:

“The biggest thing most people fail to understand is that there are a very limited number of smart, dedicated people! They can only do so many things.”

He added that if Tesla has to “maintain a complex production line, supply chain and allocate engineering for Cybertruck, we can’t use those people” for scaling Cybercab.

By this morning, the explanation had shifted again, to the “opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck.” But the Saturday version is the one that matters. Musk is telling us the bottleneck at Tesla isn’t factory space or money. It’s people.

The Cybertruck is the second casualty this year. In January, Musk announced the end of the Model S and Model X on Tesla’s Q4 earnings call and summed up the reason in one word: “Autonomy.” The Fremont line is being converted to build Optimus robots, and by April, only inventory was left.

The flagships had been on life support for years. Their last real update was the 2021 interior refresh. The June 2025 “refresh” brought a new paint color, a front bumper camera, a bit more range, and a $5,000 price increase. That’s not how you treat a vehicle program you care about.

Tesla painted a very different picture just two years ago. At its 2024 shareholder meeting, it showed this slide of its lineup: the Model 3, Model Y, Model S, Model X, Cybertruck, and Semi, plus three vehicles under covers that Musk said were “going to be pretty special.”

Of the five consumer vehicles on that slide, three are now dead or on their way out.

So here’s what will be left in the second half of 2027: Model 3 and Model Y, two vehicles built on the same platform, plus the Model Y L and cheaper “Standard” variants of both. The Semi is a commercial truck. The Roadster’s production is still a giant question mark. And the Cybercab is a robotaxi with no steering wheel, not a car you can buy – even though Tesla is going to let fleet buyers get them to add on its own Robotaxi network. We previously explained how this is a terrible idea.

For comparison, Hyundai Motor Group sells more than half a dozen EV models in the US across its Hyundai, Kia, and Genesis brands, on top of its gas and hybrid lineup. GM and Toyota run dozens of nameplates at once. Tesla can’t keep more than two programs alive at the same time.

At Tesla’s Investor Day at Giga Texas on March 1, 2023, Musk mostly stayed out of the spotlight. Instead, Tesla paraded more than a dozen executives on stage to present its plans, a rare move for a company long criticized for being a one-man show.

“We’ve obviously got significant bench strength here,” Musk said at the time.

Of the 14 executives named as presenters that day, seven are gone:

Martin Viecha, who ran investor relations through that event, left in April 2024 as well.

Seven are still at Tesla, according to their LinkedIn profiles: Tom Zhu, Lars Moravy, Franz von Holzhausen, Ashok Elluswamy, Karn Budhiraj, Laurie Shelby, and Brandon Ehrhart. And the ones who left weren’t peripheral. They ran batteries, powertrain, software, chips, energy, charging, and the money.

The bigger problem for Tesla’s ability to run vehicle programs is the program-level talent, the people who take a car from prototype to volume production.

In November 2025, Tesla lost the head of its Cybertruck program, Siddhant Awasthi, and the Model Y program manager, Emmanuel Lamacchia, within a day of each other. Lamacchia had led Tesla’s best-selling vehicle for four years.

Then the Cybercab, the program Musk is now pulling people toward, started losing its own leaders:

Add 17-year finance VP Sendil Palani and Thomas Dmytryk, the director who built Tesla’s over-the-air update system and Robotaxi infrastructure, both in March, and you get the picture.

So when Musk says he needs Cybertruck’s people for Cybercab, part of the reason is that Cybercab keeps losing its own.

Musk will frame all of this as focus. Autonomy is going to be so big, the argument goes, that Tesla has to go all in.

But we’ve heard that before. Tesla made the yoke steering wheel standard on the Model S and Model X in 2021 because the cars would soon drive themselves, then brought back a round wheel as an option. It removed the turn signal stalk from the Model 3 in 2023, then brought the stalk back in 2025 and started selling a $350 retrofit to owners. Each time, the autonomy that justified the change wasn’t there yet.

And Tesla isn’t the leader in unsupervised driving. It has the best driver-assist system on the market, but Waymo still logs roughly seven times more driverless miles per week, and NHTSA estimates Tesla’s entire Robotaxi fleet at about 1,000 vehicles. Zoox is scaling too, and Baidu’s Apollo Go runs a far bigger driverless fleet in China.

This is something that I’ve been highlighting for a decade. Even after it became a big company with a large headcount, Tesla has never been good at running several vehicle programs in a healthy way. The Model S and Model X were starved for updates long before the talent exodus started. Tesla has always thrown everything at its newest program and let the older ones coast.

What changed is that the slack is gone. In 2023, Tesla could still neglect the flagships and keep them on the market, because it had deep benches in engineering, manufacturing, and software to absorb mistakes. Today, half the executives Musk called his bench are gone, and the people running the Cybercab ramp keep walking out. Musk is now openly telling us there aren’t enough people left to build a pickup truck and a robotaxi at the same time.

Musk calls it focus. It looks a lot more like a constraint Tesla can’t hire its way out of.

Tesla never had the capacity to hire, organize, manage and retain the amount of human talent required to develop multiple car model lines in concert. Tesla barely paid its staff enough for one model line development.

You only need to look at other companies with decades of experience in developing many, separate (but technically strongly overlapping) model lines to see how much does that require in terms of human resources and in terms of R&D cost. Like BMW has always been investing ~5 billion EUR every year in R&D. That is how you have ~14 core models with at least another dozen specialist models and more regional models plus Mini and RR on top. At times up to 60 different significant variants with different drivetrains also impacting design, logistics and production. All being always in development for the next generation and also for a mid-life refresh or two. Across the whole group, including maintenance work, there can easily be triple-digit number of vehicle model projects going at the same time.

Will the Cybercab be revolutionary and make it all worth it? We have our doubts. Tesla leads in driver assistance with FSD, but it has failed to evolve the product into unsupervised self-driving at scale, which it promised to buyers for a decade. It’s clearly not the leader in unsupervised self-driving, and the competition is crowded. Tesla’s lasting impact on the robotaxi market is genuinely hard to predict.

What’s not hard to see is the trend. Tesla has shown a complete inability to sustain multiple vehicle programs at once, and it’s getting harder for the automaker, not easier. If Tesla can’t hold on to the people who build its cars, how long before the Model 3 and Model Y get the same treatment as the Model S?

Both vehicle programs will undoubtedly go down in history as some of the most critical EVs of all time, but that doesn’t guarantee lasting success in a rapidly changing auto landscape.

#4568. College student develops LEGO-like, 3D-printed moon bricks

Published Nov 10, 2026 4:30 PM EST

A permanent lunar base will require structures resilient enough to withstand everything from cosmic radiation and micro-meteorites to moonquakes. There are plenty of building materials to choose from on Earth, but they all come with a catch: transportation storage aboard spacecraft is limited, and each additional pound of cargo will quickly ramp up costs. Engineers have spent years experimenting with ways for future astronauts to source local lunar ingredients, including fine moon dust known as regolith. Unfortunately, most require various binding ingredients that must still be sent from back home.

A college student at the University of Arkansas (U of A) recently had a different idea. In a collaboration with U of A mechanical engineer Wan Shou, Cole McCallum harnessed a specialized method of 3D printing to manufacture LEGO-esque bricks from lunar dust, no binding required. (These aren’t to be confused with LEGO’s actual lunar bricks mockups). Their results published in the journal NPJ Advanced Manufacturing indicate the bricks could be a promising material to investigate as humanity readies itself for a return to the moon.

Lunar regolith is a tricky material. Unlike Earth’s dirt, it doesn’t contain any amount of organic matter. It’s just loose, sharp-edged particles generated by billions’ of years of asteroid and meteor impacts. This means that moon dust can’t bind on its own and requires at least some secondary ingredients.

While an undergraduate at the U of A, McCallum wondered if a specific type of 3D printing called laser powder bed fusion could offer a workaround. In this technique, fine powder is placed on a flat bed, then exposed to a highly powerful laser beam that fuses each microscopic particle together in a process called sintering. The tray bed lowers down to allow another layer of sintered powder, then repeats the steps until a single, solid block is created. Regolith fits the mold perfectly, so to speak.

“There’s nothing else it’s binding to. The regolith powder is binding to itself,” McCallum said in a university profile.

McCallum and Shou didn’t have access to actual lunar material, so they obtained Lunar Highlands Regolith Simulant (LHS-1), a commercial material that replicates the moon dust collected by Apollo astronauts during the 1960s and 70s. They ultimately settled on two shapes, one that resembles a cross and another that looks like the letter “H.” The researchers then 3D-printed tiny prototypes measuring a few centimeters wide that they could connect like LEGOs to construct larger structures.

There are still some important caveats to this sintered regolith strategy. McCallum’s blocks are much more porous and weaker than materials containing binders. Additional research is needed to see how the approach works in a vacuum or microgravity, two inescapable hurdles to living on the moon.

“These structures we’re making can be self-supported. But I would be hesitant to say our process could be used for something that’s supporting other loads at this moment yet,” said McCallum.

That said, his demonstration that even a basic framework for lunar base bricks is achievable solely with regolith may offer a promising direction for mission engineers

#4566. Ford’s EV batteries retain more than 90% health after 100,000 miles

Your electric vehicle battery may last longer than you think. Ford says its EV batteries retain greater than 90% health on average after 100,000 miles. Here are a few tips to keep yours healthy.

The Mustang Mach-E went on sale in late 2020 as Ford’s first fully electric crossover SUV designed from the ground up.

Since launching the 2021 Mustang Mach-E, Ford has been collecting data from over 36,000 vehicles that have traveled two billion miles across the US and Canada.

According to Ford, the Mach-E’s battery has retained 92% of its health on average over the past five years.

Across its full EV lineup, including the F-150 Lightning and E-Transit, Ford said its battery packs maintain more than 90% health on average after 100,000 miles. The key number to look at is the spread, with 95% of vehicles falling between 87% and 97% health.

Of 2021 model-year EV owners, Ford said, more than 2,000 have crossed 100,000 miles with their original battery averaging better than 91% health, while over 30 have crossed the 200,000-mile mark and average 88% health.

Ford is using real-world data to help owners take good care of their electric vehicles, no matter how much they know about batteries and other EV tech.

It’s also applying lessons from developing the Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) platform, which will underpin its next-generation EVs, starting with the Fantom pickup next year.

Ford offered a few simple, everyday tips to help owners support long-term battery health. For one, if possible, charge at home on Level 2 for daily commuting or driving and save DC fast charging for longer trips.

It also helps to avoid charging in extreme temperatures if you can. Preconditioning the battery can help bring it into the optimal temperature range, while parking in the shade on hot summer days can also help avoid long-term battery degradation.

Last, but not least, you can use the Ford App to find charge-level recommendations designed specifically for your vehicle and battery system.

The 2021 Mustang Mach-E uses an NCM battery, but some newer Ford batteries use a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery chemistry, which is recommended to charge to 100% from time to time.

Ford has introduced new features in the Ford App to help owners maintain battery health specific to their vehicle and will continue to use the data to improve the experience as it introduces its next-gen EVs.

#4565. ‘One-in-a-million’ yellow fish found in New York

Published Nov 11, 2026 8:22 AM EST

We’ll call him mellow yellow. An “exceptionally rare” yellow-colored burbot (Lota lota) was recently caught by a team of U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) biologists in Oswego Harbor on Lake Ontario in Upstate New York.

Burbots are long fish that weigh about three to five pounds on average, and live in cold rivers and lakes of North America, Europe, and Asia. To the naked eye, they appear scaleless, but are actually covered with tiny, almost microscopic scales. What they eat depends on their size. Smaller burbots will eat zooplankton, while bigger burbots prefer to snack on other fish.

The team caught the brightly colored fish during a routine aquatic invasive species survey. It gets its unique color from a rare genetic condition called xanthochromism. A genetic mutation suppresses the normal pigmentation, it produces a yellow-orange appearance instead of the burbot’s usual grey, olive, or tan coloring. In wild fish, xanthochromism is less common than albinism or melanism, making this fish an “especially unusual capture.”

The burbot is a native species in the Great Lakes, but the USFWS team says the discovery highlights the effectiveness of the Service’s Aquatic Invasive Species Early Detection and Monitoring Program. The program uses a multi-gear fish-surveillance strategy to detect certain non-native species in the harbors, rivers, and embayments of the Great Lakes. Early detection of a watchlist species gives fisheries managers the best opportunity to implement prevention and removal measures if invasive species are detected. Since invasive species are often rare when they first enter new waters, the program uses electrofishing, fyke-netting, gill-netting, and environmental DNA (eDNA) analysis to increase the chances that scientists detect an invasive species.

“The finding is notable because burbot populations in the lake are extremely low, and the species typically inhabit deeper, cooler waters than those found within the harbor,” the USFWS wrote in a statement. “It represents the first documented detection of a burbot during a fisheries survey in Oswego Harbor, although a few angler catches have been reported.”

The United States Geological Survey (USGS) fisheries biologists, who examined the fish and are familiar with the species, also observed that it was very thin and appeared to be in poor health. It was later sent to the Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine for a health analysis due to the “unexplained factors contributing to the continued suppression of its population”

“The discovery could turn out to be lucky for the burbot too; this exceptionally rare fish may provide valuable insight into the health of the species’ populations throughout the basin that can inform management actions,” the USFWS concluded.

#4564. Polestar’s Formula 2030 Concept Car Is a Futuristic Look at Tactile Driving

The concept previews the brand’s next-gen designs, which will influence new production cars in the next two years.

Polestar revealed a Formula 2030 concept car at a media drive event for the Polestar 4, and while it’s not headed for production, the electric carmaker says some of its design language will preview the next-generation Polestar 2 as well as the upcoming Polestar 7. The four-door concept has a rear hatch and is unmistakably Polestar, as evident by the brand’s signature “Dual Blade” headlights and minimalistic design. However, its low-slung profile and flared rear fenders give it an aggressive, performance-oriented silhouette.

See all results for used Polestar for sale near 07011

The car’s coach doors remove the need for a B-pillar, and the A-pillar is disguised to give the windshield and windows a wrap-around effect. Interestingly, the concept has a single windshield wiper. Glass replaces a traditional roof, and the trunk gets a large window—a stark deviation from some of Polestar’s other windowless rear ends. The trunk’s floor is also transparent, and race-inspired Öhlins dampers peek through underneath.

Polestar calls the concept’s rear end “UFO-esque.” And instead of the single long light bar that angles downward on previous models, the concept car’s lighting signature is more subtle, with just two thin taillights located under the trunk.

Nitrogen, a new exterior color that debuts on the Formula 2030 concept, shows up in three different finishes around the exterior. Polestar’s tone-in-tone treatment uses a mix of glossy, matte, and satin finishes to distinguish details like the side cladding and aero bits. Even the 22-inch wheels are color-matched, with Swedish Gold-colored Brembo brake calipers as an accent.

Inside, the four-seater continues the tone-in-tone color scheme with light-colored upholstery and gold accents in the seatbelts and controls. The seats feature inflatable bolsters and cushions that mold themselves to each occupant, and most of the interior is composed of recycled materials.

Two screens—one attached to the steering column and one in the center of the dashboard—angle toward the driver, and eight physical controls lie in the center console below the larger screen. Drivers have options for each of the controls, both in what kind of tactile control it is, like a rocker switch or dial, and what function it affects.

The center console also houses a drive-mode selector where drivers can choose between Performance, Normal, and Autonomous modes. In Performance mode, the center screen lowers to sit flush with the center console while the steering wheel and gauge screen move closer to the driver. In Autonomous mode, the car’s concealed lidar unit appears outside the car while the steering wheel and driver’s seat move further apart inside the cabin.

See all results for used Polestar for sale near 07011

The concept car wasn’t built to reach production, but Polestar has already confirmed that some of its elements will show up in the next-generation Polestar 2, which is slated to arrive in early 2027, and the upcoming Polestar 7, which is expected to arrive in 2028. Polestar is now banned from selling new vehicles in the United States, so you’ll have to head across the Atlantic to actually get your hands on Polestar’s upcoming lineup.

#4563. The electric Vespa just got better where it actually matters

Vespa’s electric scooters have never exactly screamed for attention. That’s sort of the point. They look like Vespas, ride like Vespas, and just happen to swap the gasoline engine for a much quieter electric drivetrain.

But for 2027, Vespa has given its electric lineup a fairly significant technological overhaul while leaving that iconic steel bodywork largely untouched.

Unveiled at EICMA 2026 in Milan, the new electric Vespa lineup now consists of the Primavera Elettrica, Sprint S Elettrica, and the faster Primavera Tech Elettrica. And while you’d be forgiven for struggling to spot the differences from across the show floor, there’s a lot more happening underneath.

The biggest upgrade is an entirely new electric motor developed and manufactured in Italy by Vespa parent company Piaggio Group. The motor uses a new modular design intended to improve both performance and efficiency, while also doing away with rare-earth materials.

On the 45 km/h (28 mph) Primavera and Sprint S models, Vespa says the new motor provides stronger acceleration for stop-and-go city riding. Range reaches up to 85 km (53 miles) in Eco mode.

But perhaps the biggest practical improvement is the new removable battery. Being able to pull the battery out of the scooter and carry it inside for charging makes a massive difference for urban riders who don’t have access to a garage or dedicated charging spot – exactly the kind of riders Vespa is targeting.

The Primavera Tech is where things get a little faster. This version is homologated as a motorcycle rather than a moped in Europe and reaches 67 km/h (42 mph). That’s still not terribly fast, but the electric Vespa line has never been known for its top speed.

Its range has increased by 12.5% thanks to the new motor and Vehicle Management System, reaching 90 km (56 miles) on the WMTC cycle or up to 100 km (62 miles) in Eco mode.

There’s also a new charger that Vespa says reduces energy consumption from the wall by 17%, with a 0-80% charge taking around 2.5 hours. A new Maintenance mode is designed to protect the battery during longer periods when the scooter isn’t being ridden.

Vespa is clearly only really interested in selling their gas models, which come in 50cc, 125cc, & 310cc classes. And the only reason anyone would get a 50cc is if they didn't want to bother to get an actual motorcycle license in some jurisdictions. The electrics are nearly as expensive as the 310s but even the "faster" model only has the power equivalent of about 70cc's. At least the battery in the faster model is now a decent 4.2 kwh, though that one I believe is not removable. Hey I'm actually a Vespa lover I have a 200cc. They are beautiful quality machines, and I don't mind the price premium. But the electrics are quite disappointing, especially for the money. If they had a true 125cc equivalent I would be first in line at the showroom. Very disappointing in that a stouter motor really wouldn't cost them much more at all.

The Primavera Tech also gets the technological bells and whistles you’d expect from the flagship version, including a 5-inch TFT display, keyless operation, navigation through Vespa’s smartphone connectivity system, and remote seat unlocking.

Perhaps the most Vespa thing about the whole update is how little of it you can actually see.

The company hasn’t tried to turn its electric scooters into rolling science-fiction props. They’re still unmistakably Vespas, complete with the same classic styling that has defined the brand for generations. They just happen to have a much more interesting electric drivetrain hiding underneath now.

Of course, they also carry some very Vespa pricing. While we don’t have word on the updated pricing for the new models, the outgoing Primavera Elettrica 70 RED was priced at $8,299 in the US. So don’t expect these models to come cheap.

#4562. 9-foot-tall Game Boy Color plays all the classics

Published Nov 11, 2026 8:53 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›

A pair of California-based engineers have built what they say may be the largest Game Boy Color ever. Standing more than nine feet and weighing around 300 pounds, the Pokémon-yellow goliath requires a U-Haul to transport and took over 1,500 collective hours in a makerspace to create. And it isn’t just for show. The giant handheld plays real Game Boy games, thanks to a pixel-perfect display scaled up from the original and software written from scratch. The designers even fabricated an assortment of to-scale accessories, including game cartridges, a cable link, and AA batteries.

The console has already appeared at several maker events, where eager kids have punched and kicked its chunky buttons. It has also prompted plenty of older millennials, in person and online, to reminisce about simpler days. Build videos posted across social media have racked up hundreds of thousands of views. But for co-creator Paige Powell, a veteran prop designer and mechanical engineer, the giant Game Boy also represents something more special: a labor of love and a chance to inspire young girls to start building things themselves.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

“It [has] felt very weird to me in a very male-dominated world to build something behind the scenes and then give it to [a] guy who then takes credit,” Powell tells Popular Science. “I want people to see women making stuff!”

The giant GameBoy is the joint effort of Powell (@whats_paige_making on Instagram) and engineer Nick Alvarez (@nickbuildstuff on Instagram). Powell has a long track record of building props and sets for the YouTube channel Mega Builds and the immersive art company Meow Wolf. Alvarez, meanwhile, specializes in PCB (printed circuit board) design and spent seven years as a full-time engineering manager at an aerospace defense company.

The two crossed paths while working at the Davis makerspace, just west of Sacramento. Alvarez was building a large LED wall (the kind used for screens at sports arenas) and wanted to hook up Nintendo controllers so it could play games. Piggybacking off of that, Powell proposed taking the idea a step further: a giant playable Game Boy. From there, it only made sense to try and make the world’s largest. That sent them down a rabbit hole that would consume a sizable chunk of their lives (and finances) over the months to follow.

A quick bit of research revealed they weren’t the first one with this idea. Guinness World Records actually has an official entry for the Largest Game Boy Color, an accolade claimed in 2022 by a YouTuber named Jake Carlini. His version measured in at seven feet tall. But calling that one a real Game Boy is quite a stretch. It was really little more than a few pieces of vaguely detailed plywood. Alvarez and Powell realized there was an opportunity, not just to break the record, but to build something far more ambitious.

“It [the Carlini model] was just kind of [a] slapstick way of putting it together, and we were like, ‘dude, what is this?’ Alvarez says. ”We can do something actually amazing with our background and our skillset.”

From the outset, the duo gave themselves a set of constraints to build around. Their Game Boy had to be to scale to the original and functional as a game console. They also committed to making the screen pixel perfect to the 1998 original.

“Everything was built around the constraint of what the screen was going to be,” Powell says.

Fortunately, they had some help along the way. When they told Tim Keller, the head of the Davis makerspace, about the project, he agreed to let them set up shop and use the space’s CNC mills, 3D printers, laser cutters, and other equipment.

Meet the college student crafting electric guitars from scratch

This guy crammed a laptop into an Altoids tin

Clever kid builds phone charger powered by pet hamster

Teen brothers build a Disney-inspired ride in family basement

Teen turns his suburban home into elaborate haunted house every October

In Vermont, one man is bringing pay phones back to life

With goals set and tools secured, the pair then created a 3D model of their scaled-up Game Boy, starting with a smaller (though still shockingly large) 5.7-foot version. Powell quickly realized that the toughest part to fabricate wasn’t actually the console’s iconic front, but rather its geometrically odd-shaped back shell. The top of the backside starts out flat but then bulges out into a sloped shape toward the bottom where a person would hold it in their palm. The cartridge slot where the game slides into also juts out from the back, adding even more complexity

Once the 3D model was complete, Powell began building the physical body, made mostly of plywood shaped on the CNC machine, an automated manufacturing device that reads computer code and uses that to control cutting machines like mills, lathes, and lasers. CNC machines are indispensable tools in many makers’ arsenals. But a project like this requires adaptability. Partway through, Powell says, she realized the CNC machine wasn’t all that well suited to making square cuts, which meant the final product would need more hand carpentry than initially planned.

Meanwhile, Alvarez was hard at work perfecting the display and electronics under the hood (or, in this case, the shell). He built the screen from a series of HUB75 LED panels, the kind commonly used in large digital signs. The trick was getting his massive DIY display to scale up accurately from the original GameBoy’s 160-by-144 pixel screen. He also used a small microcontroller (essentially a tiny computer assigned to a specific task) to map all of the device’s buttons and switches.

When the giant Game Boy plays games, it’s running them on a specialized emulator rather than the physical game cartridge that gets slotted into the device. The emulator is a piece of software that imitates a Game Boy. Emulators are common these days and are what let hobbyists play old Nintendo games on smartphones.

The to-scale cartridges Powell and Alvarez fabricated are really more for show. That means, theoretically, their device can run any Game Boy game. Alvarez says he even built in a feature that cycles to a different game each time the power is switched on. So far, the pair have posted videos of the device playing Pokémon and Donkey Kong. Alvarez even watched The Odyssey on it.

Powell and Alvarez have shown off their creations at two events so far: Open Sauce in 2026 and the Bay Area Maker Fair in Vallejo, California. Getting the Game Boys there was a task in itself. The larger of the two (around 300 pounds) required a large U-Haul and four people just to load it. Once unloaded, they faced a more daunting challenge: the wrath of children. Drawn in by the device’s giant buttons, kids at the events let loose.

“Kids were coming up and karate-kicking them, and I was just like, ‘Oh my God, man,’” Powell says.

Alvarez concurs. “They were punching the crap out of the buttons.”

In a testament to its build quality, the giant Game Boy withstood the onslaught of toddler haymakers. Those who weren’t assailing the device were often absorbing an emotional gut punch of their own. Both in person and online, fans told Powell and Alvarez how the build brought back childhood memories. One commenter recalled how seeing it reminded them of a time at a school when a bully stole their beloved Game Boy. Decades later, he said, he’s still mad.

Looking ahead, Powell and Alvarez hope to find their creation a new home where it can be on display and accessible to the public. They’d like to recoup some of the money they’ve poured into it, but Powell also expressed some wariness of it winding up locked away in some buyer’s private collection. Ideally, she says, it would land in a museum of some kind, where it could inspire the next generation of budding makers.

In The Workshop, Popular Science highlights the ingenious, delightful, and often surprising projects people build in their spare time. If you or someone you know is working on a hobbyist project that fits the bill, we’d love to hear about it—fill out this form to tell us more.

#4561. Rewarding for the Right Owner: 1979 Lancia Zagato Tested

The car for those who view eccentricity as a virtue and fun as a necessity.

From the May 1979 issue of Car and Driver.

“ZAG-uh-toe .... What is that, one of them new little Plymouths?”

He’d been studying the little Lancia through the window as we rummaged through his parts store in search of a you-wire-it cigarette lighter we could graft into the car’s electrical system. The on-board lighter socket had proved incompatible with our Escort’s plug.

“Za-GAH-toe,” we corrected. “It's made in Italy.”

He considered that piece of informa­tion as we paid for the lighter, then tried to sell us a can of engine additive as we made for the door. The dogeared display for the pour-in miracle claimed it would do everything short of putting you in the winner’s circle at Daytona. In the old days, in different packaging, it probably sold as a cure for rheumatism, lice, warts, heaves, halitosis, and hard hearing. He patted the uppermost can and his voice trailed us into the drizzly afternoon, hinting of impending doom.

See all results for used cars for sale near 98837

He had a point there, but we forsook the additive and let the door close be­hind us. We hooked up the Escort and set out into the growing evening rain­storm in search of a major mechanical or electrical failure to get pissed off about. The further we got from Dayto­na, spearing out into the chilly, desert­ed, water-swept two-lanes of central Florida, howling into the gloom at a steady 80, the clearer our second thoughts became. What if Lancia’s self­-incriminating talk of a “new high-quali­ty modular electrical system through­out” was just a hoax? We didn’t even have an umbrella. Would the modular electrics leave us sinking in the middle of some non-modular backwater swamp? Would the shift linkage come adrift? Would the carburetion cease to carburet, or the ignition cease to ignite? These were fits of pique visited upon us by Lancias before. But the Zagato did none of the above. Oh, the letdown, not to be able to tell you we had to hitch­hike out of the Glades in the back of a sagging half-ton Ford pickup.

Times have apparently changed at Lancia. While we can’t say the thrashing we dealt our Zagato was the equivalent of 50,000 miles’ worth of normal driv­ing, the car suffered us, if not gladly, at least with no crippling catastrophes. Its shortcomings fell more in the area of nuisance value, an area offset by the fun of driving the car under the right cir­cumstances. As often happens with cars of strong character, the Zagato’s car-to-­owner-to-car relationship becomes a high-spirited adversary relationship, an exchange of sometimes conflicting, sometime parallel philosophies. This re­lationship can make a Lancia Zagato a rewarding car for the right owner. All that remains is to determine whether ownership then qualifies him as a 24-ka­rat eccentric in good standing, or simply a lover of good fun.

See all results for used cars for sale near 98837

Fun is what Lancia had in mind when it contracted Carrozzeria Zagato to cre­ate and build a coachbuilt steel targa body for the existing Beta Coupe. The unit-bodied result is an interesting com­bination of a normal lift-off fiberglass targa roof panel and an everyday roadster’s fold-down vinyl rear roof and plastic window. The targa bar that re­mains after everything else is lifted off or folded down provides sturdy rollover protection, enhanced by horizontal out­er roofline struts that connect the bar with the windshield pillars. Four configurations are possible by adding or re­moving the roof components and roll­ing windows up or down.

The resulting greenhouse possesses all the elegance of a railroad shanty and thwarts the clean, simple lines of the lower body. From certain angles, the Zagato looks like a stubby El Camino pickup with an enclosed bed, but unlike an El Camino, it has another pair of seats behind the driver and the number­-one passenger. However, candidates for travel in back may want to suggest a democratic drawing of straws, fearing their upper and lower extremities will be forever molded into unnatural shapes. Lowering the back window pro­vides a modern version of the rumble seat and a bit more headroom, but no extra sympathy for the legs. The Zagato is not by any means or intent an appro­priate way to transport half your neigh­borhood to a formal dinner party. Con­sider it a sports car that happens to ben­efit from a slight extra people-carrying capacity suited to quick runs down to the beach, the movies, or the local wa­tering hole.

As always, Lancia has provided a nice setting for front-seat travelers, creating a modern environment that welcomes you with comfort—though the passen­ger is probably more comfortable than the driver. The seats are good, but the driver is squeezed into the classic Amer­ican-knees-in-the-American-armpits Italian driving position, arms stretching for a steering wheel that lies out near the horizon.

But inside the car, you tend to forget about the varied points of styling and sometimes even about the peculiar driv­ing position. Sometimes the Zagato is so much fun you can’t help yourself. Other people watch you rip past, and you know they’re thinking, “What would I do if I had that? What does it feel like without a roof or a back win­dow?” They figure anything with these looks must be kinda fast, and they won­der how many friends you can squeeze into the thing before the cops stop you. The Zagato is meant for the unpredict­able kind of fun you can have only if you’re unpredictable enough to have a car like this. If that’s eccentric, so be it.

The Zagato’s chassis configuration has become so commonplace as to have lost all appeal for eccentrics. Contained within the 92.5-inch wheelbase and 164.6-inch overall length are the trans­verse engine and front-wheel drive shared with Lancia’s other models, and echoed by a dozen other manufacturers. A five-speed manual or a new three-­speed automatic transmission provides the gearing, and the engine, provided by parent company Fiat, has been en­larged for all Lancia’s models this year, jumping from 1756 cc to 1995 cc. The 84.0 mm bore remains the same, but the stroke has been increased from 79.2 to 90.0 mm. The two-liter whips out 87 horsepower at an enthusiastic 5400 rpm and boasts a torque increase of almost 17 percent, up to 105 pound-feet at 2900 rpm. The double-overhead-cam four leans over twenty degrees, and its electronic ignition, Weber two-barrel carburetor, and aluminum hemi-heads provide both exotic specifications and good midrange performance. The en­gine runs on unleaded gas, purifies its wastes with a catalytic converter, and, when hitched to the five-speed over­drive, propels the Zagato an average of 19 miles per gallon.

At 2730 pounds, the Zagato is heavy for a car its size. Its standard high nu­merical gearing is necessary for lively around-town and back-road perform­ance, but it produces much noisy com­plaint from the engine in the lower gears. Fourth gear above 60 is hopelessly noisy even though it has another 27 mph worth of revs left. Fifth ceases the caterwauling up to about 70 mph, when droning sets in and wind noise around the roof panel and rear window increas­es to what seem supersonic levels. Noisy and tightly wound though it might be, the wailing little engine produces only mid-pack performance—0 to 60 mph in 11.9 seconds, the quarter-mile in 18.7 seconds at 73 mph. By standing on the gas long enough, you can wring a 103-mph top speed out of the Zagato. Its passing performance is quite reassuring when you’ve picked the right gear. On occasion, getting the right gear can be much more a bother than picking it, but the transaxle’s linkage isn’t entirely bad, and the fat shift knob and easy heel­-and-toe movement are fine. The five­-speed pattern is a proper H, with fifth up and away, opposite reverse.

The brakes Lancia has hung under the coachwork are more than just reas­suring. With a big disc at every hand­some alloy wheel, and aggressive, low­-profile Pirelli P6s, the Zagato likes nothing better than knocking off speed with breathtaking quickness and control. The speedometer needle struggles to keep up in getting down. Pedal effort is light, and the rousing 186-foot mea­surement for 70-to-0-mph stops runs neck-and-neck with or even betters some of the world’s highest-performance automobiles.

The 185/65R-14 P6 Pirellis are tre­mendous. Not only do they ride smoothly and quietly, even at the high pressures we use for hard running, they’re beyond reproach in their per­formance characteristics. They are pre­dictable, precise, and monumental in their ability to inspire confidence. They seem to have no sudden tuck-under, and finding their limit seems almost as much a mental exercise as a physical one. While the Pirellis are good, the Za­gato certainly adds its own zesty spice to the handling brew. The spring and shock rates provide a firm smoothness of control. The car’s aloof road man­ners do not disappear into the lower re­cesses of every chuckhole or flutter over every sudden rise. The suspension is all-independent, MacPherson struts all around. Each aspect of wheel control is dovetailed neatly with the others, from the point where the P6s manhandle the pavement right up to the precise, re­fined new rack-and-pinion power steer­ing, which allows only slight tugs on the wheel in the lower gears. If it were not for the power assist, the awkwardly positioned steering wheel would be a real obstacle, more opponent than ac­complice in the battle of leverage. Its rake adjustment allows none of the fore­-and-aft movement so badly needed for correct reach to the wheel.

Directional stability is outstanding, the Zagato arrowing its way over and through every snide parlor trick our grousing malcontent of a highway system can throw at it. The inherent understeer is moderate, and its symptoms are fur­ther reduced by the quick steering and the response of the Pirellis. Body roll and brake dive are under tight rein. The car works not as a scurvy rat's nest of separate parts, but as one very snug unit.

Lancia hasn’t been exactly famous for well-conceived interiors, but the Zagato benefits from a general redesign for 1979. Our white test car, trimmed in black and sporting the new bumpers and restyled grille and hood introduced this year on the older Beta Coupe, was cloaked inside with gray cut-pile carpet and black leather. The dash, also black, contains a new, six-gauge instrument panel. A 120-mph speedometer and a 7000-rpm tachometer, redlined at 6500, dominate the scene, even though they’re partly hidden behind the over­styled wheel, which has miserably placed spokes. Smaller gauges keep tabs on amps, fuel, and water temp, the oth­er three being allotted to the oil pres­sure, temperature, and level. Our water­-temp gauge wasn’t registering, so that must have meant we didn't have any . . . what, water or temp? The layout is clut­tered around the nacelle for the radio (which is very good and has a power an­tenna), but the general ergonomics and labeling of controls are excellent. The ventilation, heater, and air conditioning worked very well, handling unexpected Florida extremes in a manner obtrusive only because such adroitness was a sur­prise in a newly introduced limited-pro­duction car.

Several irritating bugaboos crop up here and there around the Zagato to take the edge off the nicer sides of its personality. A horrid “modesty panel” (the biz name for the under-dash trim panel that hides a car’s plumbing and wiring woes from critical eyes) snaps at your toes every time you press the clutch pedal, solidly and dangerously snagging your shoe as you let the pedal back out. The sun visors cannot be fold­ed to the sides. The shoulder harness has a tendency to tangle. The plastic rear window is clouded with a chemical haze. The rear-view mirror vibrates. The glove-box door fits poorly and is blemished with a bright blue “Unleaded Fuel Only” badge. And the hardware and trim don’t equal the excellent over­all paint and finish.

The Zagato, at a base price of $10,811, is about 1300 clams up on the Beta Coupe from which it springs. If its price isn’t enough to guarantee exclu­sivity to the eccentrics in its future, its availability will be: fewer than 1500 Za­gatos will be sold here. For those who can’t bear the thought of showing up at the same party with identical designer originals, a Special Edition Zagato, gild­ed in black paint, gold striping, unique emblems, and black interior, will be marketed at $11,800. Only 250 of these will find their way in.

Now all the U.S. Lancia dealers have to do is find a crowd of young, wind-in-­the-hair eccentrics who like to have fun driving fast with a carload of outdoorsy blondes over perfectly awful roads that don’t demand a lot of horsepower. Piece of cake. But they should beware of a potential buyer who sidles up looking for one of them new little Plymouths. He really just wants to unload some en­gine additive that, in a pinch, can cure hard hearing, halitosis, heaves, warts, lice, and rheumatism.

#4560. Ford May Have a Replacement for the Shelby GT350 Mustang in the Works

A report citing dealer documents claim a new naturally aspirated ‘Stang will pick up where the GT350 left off.

The sixth-generation Ford Mustang Shelby GT350 was an enthusiast’s favorite. It offered a track-ready middle ground between the standard V-8-powered GT and the supercharged Shelby GT500, with a 5.2-liter naturally aspirated “Voodoo” V-8 pumping out 526 horsepower and revving to 8250 rpm, and a 6-speed manual transmission. The GT350 left production in 2020; Ford has not replaced it with a like-for-like variant for in the current seventh-generation Mustang lineup. But that could change as soon as next year.

Ford Authority is reporting that Ford sent out dealer documents confirming a new high-performance Mustang. The new Mustang would not be called the Shelby GT350—Ford has not used Shelby branding for the S650-generation Mustang, and Shelby American is currently building its own GT350. But the new model would, it seems, fulfill that role in the lineup. (Road & Track reached out to Ford for comment on the potential new Mustang, but a spokesperson only noted the brand “can’t comment on speculation” about future vehicles.)

The report claims the new Mustang would slot between the current Mustang Dark Horse and the Dark Horse SC, and would feature either a 5.2-liter or 5.4-liter naturally aspirated V-8. A six-speed manual transmission would be available, if not the only option, and the new Mustang—unlike the Dark Horse SC—would only be available as a coupe. Per the report, it would arrive in late 2027 as a 2028 model-year vehicle and have a limited production run through the 2029 model year.

Firm performance specs were not detailed for the potential new Mustang, but Ford Authority expects the power output to be around 600 hp, slotting between the 500-hp Mustang Dark Horse and the 795-hp Mustang Dark Horse SC. No word yet on pricing, either; however, the current Mustang lineup has a large gap between the $72,760 Dark Horse Premium and the $108,085 Dark Horse SC where this vehicle would fit in nicely.

Ford has been looking at options to “expand on the Mustang family,” with reported ideas including non-traditional variants such as a four-door coupe-style sedan and even an off-road variant. Reviving the manual GT350 Mustang, at least in spirit, would counter those sacrilegious notions with some welcome red meat for enthusiasts.

#4558. Underwater internet cables can help save endangered whales

Published Nov 11, 2026 12:01 PM EST

The world’s oceans are crisscrossed by thousands of miles of deep sea fiber-optic cables. This immense infrastructure is the foundation for much of the planet’s international power transmission and telecommunications, but marine biologists say the lines can provide an unexpected conservation benefit. With a bit of creative retooling, the ocean cables can also function as surprisingly good microphones for monitoring endangered whale populations.

“This is truly exciting, as this technology enables real-time data access over tens of [miles], and from land,” said Cornell University bioacoustics researcher Léa Bouffaut.

The latest advancements were recently detailed in the journal Methods in Ecology and Evolution, and build on Bouffaut’s previous work. In 2022, her team became the first researchers to demonstrate fiber-optic cable monitoring of blue whales (Balaenoptera musculus) and fin whales (Balaenoptera physalus). The two species are respectively the largest and second-largest cetaceans, which also means they generate loud, ultra-low frequency vocalizations under 100 hertz. To record their calls, Bouffaut and colleagues utilized a system called distributed acoustic sensing (DAS). The technique works by sending laser pulses through deep sea cables using specialized equipment, which researchers then analyze for miniscule sonic alterations caused by environmental sound waves. After pinpointing blue and fin whale communications, researchers then used the cables’ positions to map the marine mammals’ movements and population distribution.

Following her initial demonstrations, Bouffaut was curious if DAS could also work for other baleen whale species. The odds necessarily weren’t in her team’s favor—smaller species like the bowhead whale (Balaena mysticetus) and critically endangered North Atlantic right whale (Eubalaena glacialis) issue calls at much higher frequencies between about 150 and 300 hertz. Their vocalizations are also less intense and travel shorter distances, making them even more difficult to parse in DAS data.

In the spring, Bouffaut traveled to the town of Utqiaġvik on Alaska’s North Slope to collaborate with the local Indigenous Iñupiat community of whalers. She also partnered with Arctic broadband company Quintillion, who provided access to one of their own deep sea telecommunications cables. Amid terabytes of DAS recordings, Bouffaut eventually achieved another first in her field. She became the first person to confirm bowhead whale vocalizations by harnessing fiber-optic cables.

“Being able to detect bowhead whales on a telecommunication cable is the proof of concept we need to show that DAS can be used to monitor all baleen whales,” explained Bouffaut.

Although the new strategy isn’t sensitive enough to replace dedicated ocean monitoring using underwater microphone arrays, Bouffaut and her colleagues believe DAS could become an invaluable additional tool. It also showcases a way to convert existing infrastructures into multi-use systems.

“The review is also a call to action for scientists, industry partners and regulators to collaborate,” said Bouffaut. “We now have the technical blueprint to turn global undersea infrastructure into a global network for ocean conservation.”

#4556. BMW Sets 2 New Nürburgring Records With Help from Pirelli

A revised semi-slick tire helped the carmaker knock down the compact car and touring car lap records at the Nordschleife.

Pirelli’s P Zero Trofeo RS is one of its most extreme performance tires, one capable of helping performance cars extract the most out of their potential. And that’s especially true when the company works with automakers directly—as the Italian rubbermaker did with BMW, developed a bespoke version specifically for the BMW M range. The new semi-slick tire remains street legal, but doesn’t sacrifice at-the-limit grip. And it helped BMW set two new ‘Ring lap records with its BMW M2 with the M Performance Track Kit and BMW M3 CS Touring.

The BMW M2 with the M Performance Track Kit managed a lap time of 7:25.068minutes. This lowered the Nürburgring Nordschleife compact car record, previously held by the M2 CS, by 0.5 seconds. The long-roof BMW M3, however, made more significant history: BMW’s M3 CS Touring lapped the 12.9-mile racetrack in 7:29.49 minutes, setting a new record for the fastest touring car ever by shaving off more than five seconds. The previous touring car lap record of 7:35.06 was held by the standard BMW M3 Touring. A combination of increased horsepower, stronger brakes, and custom rubber—as well as BMW M Development engineer Jörg Weidinger behind the wheel—pushed the wagon to success.

“The bespoke development program is the result of close collaboration between Pirelli and BMW M’s R&D teams. Thanks to advanced virtual development techniques, the two teams were able to adapt the tire’s characteristics to the different requirements from the earliest stages of the project, in line with Pirelli’s Perfect Fit approach, which aims to create products tailored to each specific model or application,” the tire maker said in a statement.

Pirelli initially tested the tires alongside BMW at the Nürburgring Nordschleife, and the tires were also later tested at the Nardò test circuit in Italy. BMW and Pirelli have collaborated on over 30 bespoke tire projects across the P Zero family over the years, and like many others, a keen eye can tell which ones are made for Bimmers; the manufacturer-specific tires feature a BMW star marking, as a nod to the integrated development process.

The woes of alternate side parking have kept his fleet moderate, with a 2014 Volkswagen Jetta GLI and a BMW 318i E30 street parked in his Queens community.

#4555. Toyota sells 3 electric SUVs, but which one is best for you?

Toyota now offers three fully electric SUVs: the bZ, C-HR, and bZ Woodland. Here’s how they stack up.

After introducing the new and improved bZ (formerly the bZ4X) in late 2025, the electric SUV quickly became one of the most popular EVs in the US.

In the first nine months of 2026, it was the fourth-best-selling electric vehicle, behind the Hyundai IONIQ 5, Tesla Model 3, and Tesla Model Y.

With two additional electric SUVs now on sale, the CH-R and bZ Woodland, Toyota has suddenly become one of America’s top-selling EV brands.

Its EV sales have nearly tripled this year. According to Cox Automotive, Toyota ranked as the third most popular EV brand behind Tesla and Rivian in the third quarter.

Toyota offers three distinct electric vehicles: the 2027 bZ, C-HR, and bZ Woodland, each designed for different lifestyles, so which one is the best fit for you?

After launching the updated model last year, the 2027 bZ starts at $34,980. With the $1,595 delivery fee, the starting price is $36,576.

That’s for the standard 2027 Toyota bZ XLE FWD with an EPA-estimated driving range of up to 236 miles. For longer range, you can upgrade to the FWD Plus model, which offers up to 314 miles and starts at $37,980 (excluding the delivery fee).

The Toyota bZ is available in XLE and Limited grades, with front- or all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrains.

Two battery options are offered: The 57.7 kWh battery on the standard XLE FWD provides an EPA-estimated range of up to 236 miles, while the larger 74.7 kWh battery provides up to 288 miles of range on the XLE AWD and 314 miles on the XLE FWD Plus model.

FWD models produce either 165 hp (XLE FWD) or 221 hp (XLE FWD Plus and Limited FWD), while AWD models deliver a combined 338 hp.

The 2027 bZ also has a built-in NACS port, so you can use Tesla Superchargers without needing a separate adapter. Toyota said it takes around 30 minutes to charge the battery from 10% to 80%.

Inside, the 2027 bZ features Toyota’s updated cabin design. The setup features a 7″ LCD customizable Multi Information Display (MID) and a new 14″ Toyota Audio Multimedia display screen with wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

The bZ is essentially designed as an everyday driver with a long driving range, modern tech, and available AWD.

For those looking for a bigger, more rugged option, the 2027 bZ Woodland may be a better fit. The Woodland is 6″ longer than the standard bZ and comes with standard AWD.

The longer body opens up more interior space, with up to 74.3 cubic feet of storage compared to the bZ with up to 67.1 cubic feet.

Unlike the bZ, the Woodland model has a standard AWD powertrain with Toyota’s X-Mode control system.

The setup delivers a combined 375 horsepower, 37 hp more than the standard bZ, making it Toyota’s most powerful EV currently.

It also adopts a more commanding, upright stance with 8.3″ of ground clearance and 3,500 lbs of towing capacity.

Although it uses the same 74.7 kWh battery as the standard bZ, the Woodland’s EPA-estimated range drops to 281 miles because of the added weight and power. Upgrading to the optional all-terrain tires sacrifices even more range, with up to 260 miles.

Like the bZ, the Woodland also has a built- in NACS port. Charging the battery from 10% to 80% takes around 30 minutes.

Inside, the bZ Woodland features the same 7″ LCD customizable Multi Information Display (MID) and 14″ Toyota Audio Multimedia display screen with wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

The 2027 Toyota bZ Woodland is available in Base and Premium trims, starting at $45,380. All variants include standard roof rails, Dual Qi-capable wireless device chargers, heated front seats and steering wheel, and Digital Key capabilities.

Last, but not least, the C-HR is a smaller, sporty, coupe-like electric SUV. The 2027 Toyota C-HR starts at $37,080, or $2,100 more than the standard bZ.

It’s about 6.7″ shorter than the bZ, with a smaller wheelbase, but also comes with standard AWD. The dual-motor AWD setup delivers a combined 338 hp, not quite as much as the bigger, more powerful Woodland.

The C-HR is available exclusively with the 74.7 kWh battery, which provides an EPA-estimated range of up to 287 miles for the SE grade with 18″ wheels.

Upgrading to 20″ wheels adds a street-ready look but offers slightly less EPA range, with up to 273 miles.

The coupe-like design adds a sleek look and opens up interior space, with up to 59.5 cubic feet of rear cargo space when the rear seats are folded. That’s slightly more than the bZ, which offers up to 56.9 cubic feet.

Inside, the C-HR features the same setup as its other EVs, including a 7″ slim driver’s display and 14″ central infotainment screen.

Like Toyota’s other electric SUVs, the C-HR has a native NACS port. Charging the battery from 10% to 80% takes about 30 minutes.

These are all basically the same small vehicles. I did not fit in any of them (6’ 2”) it is so frustrating to have less than 300 miles of range on AWD versions that are supposed to be better models.

It is 2026 over a decade since EVs arrived and over 5 years after the Tesla Model Y with practically zero competition almost at same price (Rivian R2 may be next year when affordable versions ship.) BMW, Mercedes and Volvo need $10k more. Hyundai has kept EV5 out of USA.

It is almost like none of the Legacy automakers want any SUV that can compete on price.

The 2027 Toyota C-HR EV is available in two trims: SE and XSE. Standard features include two wireless Qi phone chargers, low-profile roof rails, Fabric/SofTex-trimmed seating, heated front seats and steering wheel, Toyota Safety Sense 3.0, and a power liftgate.

#4554. Chunky mama bear wins 2026 Nope award for quick retreat from bigger rival

Published Nov 11, 2026 1:12 PM EST

Despite both species being bears, black bears (Ursus americanus) typically won’t go to areas that brown bears (Ursus arctos) frequent. For one, brown bears are bigger, at 600 to 900 pounds to the black bear’s average of 90 to 500 pounds.

Despite her large stature (and award-winning butt), a mother bear in Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska named Volverine instantly turned around when she noticed a female brown bear named Bullseye standing right behind her. The U.S. Forest Service team at Tongass National Forest has awarded her the 2026 Nope Award for her quick turn away from Bullseye.

“It took a minute for Volverine to notice Bullseye the brown bear standing right behind her, but when she saw, she said, ‘Nope!’” the rangers write.

Bullseye is a five-year-old brown bear who is known for dark circles around her eyes, and dark brown fur mixed into her blonde coat. And if you are keeping score at home, this is Volverine’s second award this season. She also won the 2026 Big & Beautiful Award for her beautiful bulky body.

The rangers at Tongass National Forest are currently awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States, and covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendanhall Glacier (a popular destination for tourists on Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears on the hunt for food. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. As such, the creek is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears like Volverine and eight brown bears like Bullseye. Similar to  their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their antics.
